etymology: From Chalcedon, the city near Constantinople where the fourth ecumenical council met in 451, + definition (Latin definire, to mark the bounds); the council's settled statement of the person of Christ.
biblical_def: The Chalcedonian Definition is the statement of the person of Christ set forth by the Council of Chalcedon in A.D. 451, the fourth ecumenical council, and received ever since by Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant alike as the boundary-stone of orthodox Christology. Against Nestorius, who so divided the two natures as to make two persons, and against Eutyches, who so mingled them as to swallow the human in the divine, the council confessed one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man, of a reasonable soul and body; consubstantial with the Father as to His Godhead and consubstantial with us as to His manhood; to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The two natures are not blended into a third thing, nor are they torn into two persons; the distinction of natures is preserved, and both concur in one person and one subsistence. These four negatives — without confusion, change, division, separation — are the four walls that guard the mystery of the incarnation. This dictionary confesses the Chalcedonian Definition without reservation as a faithful drawing-out of what the Scriptures teach of the God-man, and the 1689 Confession rests on it.
webster_summary: The fourth ecumenical council's statement (A.D. 451) of the person of Christ: one Son, truly God and truly man, in two natures — without confusion, change, division, or separation. The boundary-stone of orthodox Christology, confessed by the whole church.
webster_full: CHALCEDONIAN DEFINITION, noun. The Christological statement of the Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451.
Confesses one Son, Jesus Christ, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man.
He is consubstantial with the Father in Godhead and consubstantial with us in manhood.
Acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.
Received by the whole church as the boundary of orthodox Christology.
scriptures: John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Phil 2:6
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Heb 2:17
Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God.
corruption_summary: Every age finds a way to refuse the God-man — ancient heresies divided or mingled His natures; modern liberalism reduces Him to a good man only, and the prosperity and progressive pulpits make Him a symbol, a coach, or a projection of the self — all of them denying the one Lord Chalcedon confessed.
corruption_paragraphs: Chalcedon was framed against two corruptions still with us. Nestorianism so separated the natures as to deny that the one who suffered was God in the flesh; modern theologies that speak of a merely human Jesus indwelt by the divine repeat its error. Eutychianism so mingled the natures as to make a third hybrid thing that is neither God nor man; modern theologies that dissolve Christ's true humanity into a vague divinity repeat its error. The four negatives — without confusion, change, division, separation — cut off both.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the council's text, but it faces the constant pressure to reduce the incarnate Lord to something the age can manage: a moral teacher, a liberator-figure, a screen for the self. The principle to recover is the full confession: the Word was made flesh (John 1:14), in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9), yet He was made like His brethren in all things (Heb 2:17). Salvation hangs on this — only one who is truly God and truly man could reconcile God and man.
roots_summary: From Chalcedon (the council city) + Latin definire (to mark the bounds); the 451 confession of one Christ in two unconfused, unmingled natures.
roots_lines: Chalcedon — the city near Constantinople where the council met in A.D. 451
Latin definire, to set the boundaries
Framed against Nestorius (two persons) and Eutyches (mingled natures)
The four negatives: without confusion, change, division, separation
One person, two natures — truly God and truly man
usage: The Chalcedonian Definition guards the mystery of the incarnation with four negatives.
Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant alike confess the Chalcedonian Definition of Christ's person.
To deny the Chalcedonian Definition is to lose either Christ's deity or His humanity, and so the gospel.

etymology: From Ephesus, the city in Asia Minor where the third ecumenical council met in 431, + council (Latin concilium, an assembly called together).
biblical_def: The Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, met in A.D. 431 in the city famous for Paul's long ministry and John's later care, to judge the teaching of Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople. Nestorius had objected to calling the Virgin Mary Theotokos, "God-bearer," preferring Christotokos, "Christ-bearer," because he so divided the divine and human in Christ that he seemed to make two persons loosely joined — as if the man Jesus and the divine Word were two who cooperated, rather than one Lord. Cyril of Alexandria led the orthodox answer: the one born of Mary is truly the eternal Son, so that Mary may rightly be called God-bearer — not because she is the source of His deity, but because the child she bore is, in one person, very God. The council condemned Nestorius and affirmed the unity of Christ's person. This dictionary receives Ephesus's central judgment — that the one Christ is a single person, true God and true man — as biblical and necessary, the road that led to Chalcedon. It guards Theotokos strictly as a statement about Christ, never as a warrant for the Marian devotion that later corruption built upon it.
webster_summary: The third ecumenical council (A.D. 431) that condemned Nestorius and affirmed the unity of Christ's person, defending the title Theotokos ("God-bearer") as a true confession that the child of Mary is, in one person, very God. A statement about Christ, not a charter for Marian devotion.
webster_full: COUNCIL OF EPHESUS, noun. The third ecumenical council, held at Ephesus in A.D. 431.
Summoned to judge the teaching of Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople.
Led by Cyril of Alexandria, it condemned Nestorius's division of Christ into two persons.
It affirmed Theotokos ("God-bearer") as a true confession about the one person of Christ.
A step on the road to the Chalcedonian Definition of 451.
scriptures: Luke 1:43
And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
Gal 4:4
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law.
John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Matt 1:23
Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
corruption_summary: The true confession of Ephesus — that Mary's child is God — was later twisted into the corruption of Marian devotion, exalting the mother in place of honoring the Son; the modern error runs the other way, dividing Christ into a merely human Jesus and an abstract divine principle.
corruption_paragraphs: The word Theotokos was never meant to exalt Mary; it was meant to confess Christ. To say Mary is God-bearer is to say the infant in her arms is God the Son, Emmanuel, God with us (Matt 1:23). The corruption came when later Rome and the East built upon this true word a whole edifice of Marian devotion, prayer to Mary, her immaculate conception and bodily assumption, and her coronation as Queen of Heaven — honors Scripture gives to no creature. The dictionary keeps the Christological confession and rejects the devotion built on it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the council's judgment, but Nestorius's old error has modern heirs — those who split the Lord into the human Jesus of history and a divine Christ of faith, two figures loosely related. The principle to recover is the unity of Christ's person: the eternal Word (John 1:1) was made of a woman (Gal 4:4), and Elizabeth rightly called Mary "the mother of my Lord" (Luke 1:43) — one Lord, one person, true God and true man.
roots_summary: From Ephesus (the council city) + Latin concilium (assembly); the 431 council that affirmed the unity of Christ's person and the title Theotokos against Nestorius.
roots_lines: Ephesus — the city of Paul's ministry and the council of A.D. 431
Latin concilium, an assembly called together
Greek Theotokos, "God-bearer" — a confession about Christ
Condemned Nestorius's division of Christ into two persons
Led by Cyril of Alexandria; a step toward Chalcedon
usage: The Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorius and confessed the unity of Christ's person.
At Ephesus, Theotokos meant that Mary's child is very God, not that Mary is to be worshipped.
Cyril led the Council of Ephesus to guard the one Lord against a divided Christ.

etymology: From Trent (Trento, in northern Italy), where the council sat in three periods between 1545 and 1563, + council (Latin concilium); the Roman church's answer to the Reformation.
biblical_def: The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the Roman Catholic Church's formal answer to the Protestant Reformation, the engine of the Counter-Reformation, sitting in three periods at Trent in northern Italy. Far from yielding to the recovered gospel, Trent fixed Rome's opposition to it in dogmatic decrees and canons that remain binding Catholic doctrine to this day. Against sola Scriptura it set Scripture and unwritten tradition as equal sources, and made the church the authoritative interpreter, adding the Apocrypha to the canon. Against sola fide it anathematized justification by faith alone, teaching instead a justification by faith joined to infused righteousness and sustained by works and the sacraments, which can be lost and regained through the confessional. It reaffirmed the seven sacraments, transubstantiation, the sacrifice of the Mass, purgatory, indulgences, the invocation of saints, and the treasury of merit. With pointed canons it pronounced its anathema — "let him be accursed" — upon the very heart of the Reformation gospel. This dictionary therefore names Trent not as a reform but as the dogmatic entrenchment of the corruptions the Reformation called the church away from, and its anathemas against justification by faith alone as the council's most grievous error.
webster_summary: The Roman church's answer to the Reformation (1545–63): it set tradition equal with Scripture, anathematized justification by faith alone, and reaffirmed the Mass, transubstantiation, purgatory, indulgences, and the invocation of saints — entrenching, not reforming, the corruptions the Reformation opposed.
webster_full: COUNCIL OF TRENT, noun. The Roman Catholic council of 1545–1563, engine of the Counter-Reformation.
Set Scripture and unwritten tradition as equal authorities; added the Apocrypha to the canon.
Anathematized justification by faith alone, teaching infused righteousness sustained by works and sacraments.
Reaffirmed transubstantiation, the sacrifice of the Mass, purgatory, indulgences, and the invocation of saints.
Pronounced its anathema on the heart of the Reformation gospel; its decrees still bind Rome.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
corruption_summary: Modern ecumenism labors to read Trent and Vatican II as having quietly resolved the Reformation dispute, so that Protestants and Rome now agree on justification; this is not granted — Trent's anathemas against faith alone have never been revoked and stand on the books.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption Trent fixed in place is the denial of justification by faith alone. Where Paul declares that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law (Rom 3:28) and that God justifies the ungodly who believes (Rom 4:5), Trent pronounced its curse on this very doctrine and taught a justification mixed with works and lost through mortal sin. The Reformation did not invent a new gospel at this point; it recovered the old one, and Trent cursed it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the council's decrees, which are public and binding. The modern corruption is ecumenical: the claim that the Joint Declaration on Justification and the spirit of Vatican II have dissolved the old dispute. But Trent's canons still stand, anathema and all, and Paul's warning binds the church — if any preach another gospel, let him be accursed (Gal 1:8). The principle to recover is that justification by faith alone is the article on which the church stands or falls, not a misunderstanding to be smoothed over.
roots_summary: From Trent (the Italian city) + Latin concilium (council); the 1545–63 Counter-Reformation council that anathematized the Reformation gospel.
roots_lines: Trent (Trento), northern Italy — the council sat there 1545–1563
Latin concilium, an assembly; the engine of the Counter-Reformation
Set tradition equal with Scripture; added the Apocrypha
Anathematized justification by faith alone (against Rom 3:28)

usage: The Council of Trent answered the Reformation not by reform but by curse.
Trent's anathema fell on the very doctrine of justification by faith alone (Rom 3:28).
Modern ecumenism cannot dissolve the Council of Trent, whose canons still bind Rome.

etymology: From the Lateran palace in Rome (named for the ancient Laterani family), where the council met in 1215, + council; the great medieval council under Pope Innocent III.
biblical_def: The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, summoned by Pope Innocent III at the height of medieval papal power, was the most important council of the Western church between antiquity and Trent, and the one in which several of the corruptions the Reformation later opposed were given their fixed dogmatic form. It was here that the word transubstantiation was first made official doctrine — the teaching that in the Mass the substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood while the appearances remain. The council required every Christian to confess his sins to a priest at least once a year and to receive the Eucharist at Easter, fastening the auricular confession upon the conscience of Christendom. It defined the seven sacraments as the channels of grace, asserted the universal jurisdiction of the Roman see, and ordered measures against the Albigensian and Waldensian dissenters and harsh restrictions upon the Jews. This dictionary names the Fourth Lateran Council as a chief source of the very errors the Reformation called the church away from — transubstantiation above all — while recognizing that it acted within a church that still held the Trinity, the incarnation, and the Chalcedonian faith.
webster_summary: The great medieval council of 1215 under Innocent III that first made transubstantiation official dogma, required yearly auricular confession to a priest, and asserted the universal jurisdiction of the Roman see — fixing several of the corruptions the Reformation later opposed.
webster_full: FOURTH LATERAN COUNCIL, noun. The council of 1215 summoned by Pope Innocent III at the height of papal power.
First made transubstantiation official Roman dogma.
Required yearly confession to a priest and Easter communion of every Christian.
Defined the seven sacraments and asserted the universal jurisdiction of the Roman see.
Ordered measures against the Albigensians, Waldensians, and the Jews.
scriptures: 1 Tim 2:5
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.
1 John 1:9
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
John 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
corruption_summary: The Fourth Lateran Council is itself a monument of corruption — it dogmatized transubstantiation, bound the conscience to priestly confession, and exalted the papal see; the modern temptation is to honor it as a high point of unified Christendom and forget what it fastened on the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption fixed at Lateran IV is threefold. Transubstantiation turned the Lord's Supper into a recurring sacrifice and a miracle worked by the priest, against the once-for-all offering by which Christ has perfected forever them that are sanctified (Heb 10:14). Auricular confession to a priest as the appointed channel of forgiveness obscured the one Mediator (1 Tim 2:5) and the believer's direct confession to God (1 John 1:9). And the claim of universal papal jurisdiction exalted a man into an office Scripture gives to none.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the council's canons. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Christ's one offering and His one mediation: the believer needs no priest but Christ, no sacrifice but Calvary, and no absolution but the free forgiveness God gives to those who confess to Him. Lateran IV shows how far a church may drift from the simplicity of the gospel even while keeping the ancient creeds; the Reformation's work was to call her back.
roots_summary: From the Lateran palace in Rome + Latin concilium (council); the 1215 council under Innocent III that dogmatized transubstantiation and required yearly priestly confession.
roots_lines: The Lateran palace in Rome, seat of the medieval popes

Asserted the universal jurisdiction of the Roman see
usage: The Fourth Lateran Council made transubstantiation the official doctrine of Rome.
It was the Fourth Lateran Council that bound yearly confession to a priest upon Christendom.
The errors of the Fourth Lateran Council were among those the Reformation called the church away from.

etymology: From Constantinople, the imperial city where the second ecumenical council met in 381, named for the emperor Constantine; the council that completed the Nicene Creed.
biblical_def: The Council of Constantinople of A.D. 381, the second ecumenical council, summoned by the emperor Theodosius, completed the work begun at Nicaea fifty-six years before and gave the church the creed she confesses to this day. Nicaea (325) had confessed the Son to be homoousios, of one substance with the Father, true God of true God, against the Arians who made Him a creature. But the Arian struggle dragged on, and a new error arose — the Pneumatomachi, the "Spirit-fighters," who denied the full deity of the Holy Spirit. Constantinople answered, led by the labors of the Cappadocian fathers (Basil, the two Gregories), confessing the Holy Spirit to be the Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified. So the church confessed the full and equal deity of the third Person and rounded out the doctrine of the Trinity: one God in three Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed that resulted is received by the whole church. This dictionary confesses it without reservation as a faithful expression of the Scripture's teaching on the triune God.
webster_summary: The second ecumenical council (A.D. 381) that completed the Nicene Creed, confessing the full deity of the Holy Spirit against the Pneumatomachi and rounding out the doctrine of the Trinity — one God in three Persons. The work of the Cappadocian fathers, received by the whole church.
webster_full: COUNCIL OF CONSTANTINOPLE (381), noun. The second ecumenical council, summoned by Theodosius.
Completed the creed begun at Nicaea (325).
Answered the Pneumatomachi ("Spirit-fighters") who denied the Spirit's deity.
Confessed the Holy Spirit as Lord and Giver of life, worshipped with Father and Son.
Shaped by the Cappadocian fathers; gave the church the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed.
scriptures: Matt 28:19
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
Acts 5:3
But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost... thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
John 15:26
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me.
corruption_summary: The ancient Spirit-fighters who denied the deity of the Holy Ghost have modern heirs in every theology that reduces the Spirit to a force, an influence, or an impersonal energy; and the modern charismatic excess errs the other way, exalting experiences of the Spirit above the Word He inspired.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Constantinople answered was the denial of the Spirit's full deity — the Pneumatomachi who would grant the Son His Godhead but not the Spirit. Scripture forbids the reduction: to lie to the Holy Ghost is to lie to God (Acts 5:3); the one name into which we are baptized is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (Matt 28:19); the apostolic blessing joins the three (2 Cor 13:14). The Spirit is no force or influence but the third Person, the Lord and Giver of life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the creed, but the Spirit is dishonored in two modern ways. Liberal and quasi-pantheist theology dissolves Him into an impersonal energy; some charismatic excess detaches Him from the Word He inspired, exalting raw experience and new revelations over the closed canon. The principle to recover is the creed's own confession: the Holy Spirit is true God, worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son, and He testifies not of Himself but of Christ (John 15:26).
roots_summary: From Constantinople (the imperial city) + the council of 381; completed the Nicene Creed by confessing the deity of the Holy Spirit and the full doctrine of the Trinity.

At Constantinople the church confessed the Holy Spirit to be Lord and Giver of life.
The Cappadocian fathers carried the day at Constantinople against the Spirit-fighters.

etymology: From apostolic (of the apostles, Greek apostolos, one sent) + fathers; the earliest Christian writers after the apostles, some of whom knew them.
biblical_def: The Apostolic Fathers are the earliest Christian writers after the New Testament, men of the late first and early second centuries, some of whom had known the apostles or their hearers, and whose writings give the first uninspired witness to the faith once delivered. Among them are Clement of Rome, whose letter to the Corinthians (c. A.D. 96) urges order and humility on a divided church; Ignatius of Antioch, who wrote seven letters on his road to martyrdom in Rome, longing to be ground as wheat for Christ; Polycarp of Smyrna, the disciple of John, who at his own burning declared that eighty-six years he had served Christ who never did him wrong; the unknown author of the Didache, an early manual of church order; and the writers of the Epistle of Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas. Their writings are not Scripture, and they already show the seeds of later development — a rising emphasis on the single bishop, a growing legalism, allegorical excess — which the dictionary marks honestly. Yet they bear precious early testimony to the apostolic gospel, the deity of Christ, the resurrection, and the costliness of confessing the Lord. This dictionary honors them as faithful early witnesses, weighed always by the inspired Word they followed.
webster_summary: The earliest Christian writers after the apostles (c. A.D. 90–150) — Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, the Didache — some of whom knew the apostles. Precious early witnesses to the gospel, though not Scripture, and already showing the seeds of later development.
webster_full: APOSTOLIC FATHERS, noun. The earliest Christian writers after the New Testament, c. A.D. 90–150.
Some knew the apostles or their hearers; they give the first uninspired witness to the faith.
Clement of Rome wrote to the Corinthians; Ignatius of Antioch wrote seven letters toward martyrdom.
Polycarp of Smyrna, disciple of John, was burned for confessing Christ.
Their writings are not Scripture, and already show the seeds of later development.
scriptures: 2 Thess 2:15
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
Jude 3
ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
2 Tim 2:2

corruption_summary: Two corruptions surround the Apostolic Fathers: Rome and the East raise their early witness to near-Scripture and read the later episcopal and sacramental system back into them, while liberal scholarship uses their differences from the apostles to argue that there was never one apostolic gospel at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman corruption presses the Apostolic Fathers into service for the later system: Clement's call to order becomes proof of a Roman primacy he never claimed; Ignatius's zeal for the bishop becomes the monarchical episcopate and, eventually, the papacy. The dictionary reads them as they are — early, fallible, sub-apostolic witnesses — and refuses to let later developments be smuggled back into the first century.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the texts, but liberal scholarship works the opposite mischief, magnifying every difference between the Fathers and the apostles to deny that there was ever a single deposit of faith. The principle to recover is that the faith was once delivered to the saints (Jude 3), and these men, for all their imperfection, are to be weighed by that deposit — their faith followed where it follows Christ (Heb 13:7), and corrected where it strays. They committed to faithful men what they had received (2 Tim 2:2); we receive their witness gratefully and test it by the Word.
roots_summary: From Greek apostolos (one sent) + fathers; the earliest sub-apostolic Christian writers, weighed always by the inspired Word.
roots_lines: Greek apostolos, one sent — of the apostles or their hearers
The earliest Christian writers after the New Testament, c. A.D. 90–150
Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp of Smyrna
The Didache, Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas
Witnesses, not Scripture — weighed by the faith once delivered (Jude 3)
usage: The Apostolic Fathers give the church her first uninspired witness to the apostolic gospel.
Polycarp, one of the Apostolic Fathers, was the disciple of the apostle John.
The dictionary weighs the Apostolic Fathers by the Scripture they followed, never above it.

etymology: From Alexandria, the great Egyptian city of learning, + school; the early Christian center of theology and interpretation associated with Clement, Origen, Athanasius, and Cyril.
biblical_def: The Alexandrian School was the early Christian center of learning at Alexandria in Egypt, the most famous seat of scholarship in the ancient world, which shaped Christian theology for good and ill from the second through the fifth centuries. Its catechetical school produced both treasure and error. Clement of Alexandria and especially Origen pioneered Christian scholarship, textual labor, and the defense of the faith against pagan philosophy — but Origen also wove in speculations the church later condemned: the pre-existence of souls, a tendency toward universal restoration, and an allegorical method that too often loosed the text from its plain sense. Yet from the same Alexandria came mighty defenders of orthodoxy: Athanasius, who stood against the world for the deity of the Son when the whole empire went Arian, and Cyril, who at Ephesus guarded the unity of Christ's person against Nestorius. The Alexandrian tendency in Christology stressed the oneness of Christ (over against the Antiochene stress on the distinction of His natures), a stress that, pressed too far in others, slid toward the Eutychian error Chalcedon rejected. This dictionary honors Alexandria's Athanasius and Cyril as champions of the faith, while marking Origen's speculations and the school's allegorical excess as errors to be weighed and, where needful, rejected.
webster_summary: The early Christian school of learning at Alexandria, source of both treasure and error: Origen's scholarship and his condemned speculations; Athanasius's defense of Christ's deity and Cyril's defense of His one person; and an allegorical method that often loosed the text from its plain sense.
webster_full: ALEXANDRIAN SCHOOL, noun. The early Christian center of theology and interpretation at Alexandria in Egypt.
Produced Clement and Origen — pioneers of scholarship, but Origen also of condemned speculations.
Gave the church Athanasius, defender of the Son's deity against Arianism.
Gave the church Cyril, defender of Christ's one person against Nestorius.
Marked by an allegorical method that often loosed the text from its plain sense.
scriptures: John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
2 Cor 4:2
not handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
John 5:39

corruption_summary: The Alexandrian allegorical method, when loosed from the text's plain meaning, became a fountain of error — reading hidden senses into every word and burying the literal truth; the modern heirs of that loosing are the critics and the spiritualizers who likewise make the text say whatever they please.
corruption_paragraphs: The lasting corruption of the Alexandrian School is its allegorical excess. Origen could read almost any passage as a hidden spiritual cipher, and in his hands the plain historical and grammatical sense too often vanished. With it came real heresy: the pre-existence of souls and a leaning toward the universal restoration of all things, including, in some readings, the devil himself — teachings the church later condemned. The dictionary keeps what is sound in Alexandria and rejects these speculations by name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the school's history, but its loosing of interpretation from the plain text has modern children: the critic who makes the Bible a quarry for whatever theory he brings, and the spiritualizer who finds private meanings the text never bore. The principle to recover is honest interpretation — not handling the word of God deceitfully (2 Cor 4:2), but reading it in its plain grammatical and historical sense, by which the unstable wrest the Scriptures to their own destruction (2 Pet 3:16) only when they abandon it. Athanasius and Cyril, Alexandria's glory, defended truths the text plainly teaches.
roots_summary: From Alexandria (the Egyptian city) + school; the early Christian seat of learning, source of Athanasius and Cyril, but also of Origen's speculation and allegorical excess.

The Christian catechetical school of Clement and Origen

Marked by an allegorical method prone to loosing the plain sense
usage: The Alexandrian School gave the church Athanasius and Cyril, and also Origen's errors.

Against the Antiochene stress on Christ's two natures, the Alexandrian School stressed His one person.

etymology: Paul, bishop of Antioch, called "of Samosata" from his birthplace on the Euphrates; a third-century teacher condemned for denying the true deity of Christ.
biblical_def: Paul of Samosata was bishop of Antioch in the latter half of the third century and one of the early heretics whom the church condemned for denying the eternal deity of the Son. His error was a form of what is called Monarchianism or adoptionism: to guard the oneness of God, he taught that the Word and the Spirit were not distinct Persons but powers of the one God; that Jesus was a mere man, born of Mary, upon whom the divine Word or Wisdom rested as an indwelling power; and that this man, by his obedience, was exalted and adopted into a kind of divine sonship — not the eternal Son made flesh, but a man taken up. He is reported also to have lived in worldly pomp and to have suppressed hymns that praised Christ as God. The Synods of Antioch examined him and, about A.D. 268, deposed and excommunicated him; he clung to his see only under the protection of Queen Zenobia of Palmyra until Rome retook the city. His memory remained a watchword for the adoptionist heresy, and his case sharpened the church's confession of the eternal, true, and proper deity of the Son. This dictionary names his teaching as a denial of Christ that empties the gospel of its Savior.
webster_summary: A third-century bishop of Antioch condemned for adoptionism — the denial that Jesus is the eternal Son made flesh, teaching instead that He was a mere man upon whom the divine Word rested as a power and who was exalted to sonship. Deposed by the Synods of Antioch (c. A.D. 268).

Taught a form of Monarchianism / adoptionism to guard the oneness of God.
Denied that the Word and Spirit are distinct Persons; made Jesus a mere man indwelt by a divine power.
Taught that this man was exalted and adopted into divine sonship, not the eternal Son incarnate.
Deposed and excommunicated by the Synods of Antioch, c. A.D. 268.

corruption_summary: The adoptionism of Paul of Samosata — Jesus a good man whom God exalted, not God the Son made flesh — never died; it lives in every modern theology that honors Jesus as the best of men, a divine teacher, or a Spirit-filled prophet, while denying that He is, in His own person, eternal God.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption of Paul of Samosata is adoptionism: the denial that the Son is eternally and truly God, replacing the incarnation of the eternal Word with the exaltation of a mere man. Scripture leaves no room for it. The Word who was made flesh was, in the beginning, God (John 1:1, 14); the Son says "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58); He is before all things, and by Him all things consist (Col 1:17). A Christ who began as a man and was promoted to deity is not the Christ of the Bible and cannot save.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the historical record, but Samosata's heresy has many living heirs: liberal Christologies that make Jesus a uniquely God-conscious man, Unitarian denials of His deity, and the cults that crown Him a created exalted being. The principle to recover is the eternal, true, and proper deity of the Son — not adopted but begotten, not exalted into Godhead but eternally God, made flesh for our salvation. The church deposed Paul of Samosata because the gospel itself was at stake.
roots_summary: Paul, bishop of Antioch, "of Samosata" (his birthplace on the Euphrates); a third-century adoptionist who denied the eternal deity of the Son.

etymology: Aurelius Augustinus, bishop of Hippo Regius in North Africa (354–430); the greatest of the Latin fathers and a chief fountain of later Reformed theology.
biblical_def: Augustine of Hippo (354–430), bishop of Hippo Regius in Roman North Africa, was the greatest of the Latin fathers and, after the apostles, perhaps the single most influential theologian of the Western church — the man the Reformers cited more than any other outside Scripture. Born to a pagan father and the praying Monica, he wandered through worldly ambition, a long bondage to lust, and the Manichaean heresy before his famous conversion in a Milan garden, where the words "take up and read" led him to Romans 13 and to Christ. His Confessions traces the sovereign grace that pursued him; his City of God set the two cities, earthly and heavenly, against the ruin of Rome. Against Pelagius, who taught that man could obey God by his own free will without grace, Augustine recovered the biblical doctrines of original sin, the bondage of the fallen will, the necessity of efficacious grace, and predestination according to God's good pleasure — the very doctrines the Reformation would recover again. He was not free of error: his sacramentalism, his reading of the church, and his over-allegorizing fed later Roman corruptions. But on sin and grace he is the fountainhead the Reformers drank from, and this dictionary honors him as the doctor of grace.
webster_summary: The greatest of the Latin fathers (354–430), bishop of Hippo, whose Confessions and City of God shaped the Western church. Against Pelagius he recovered original sin, the bondage of the will, efficacious grace, and predestination — the doctor of grace the Reformers cited most. Honored here, though not free of error.

The fountainhead the Reformers drank from, though not free of sacramental and allegorical error.

corruption_summary: Augustine is corrupted by selective claiming: Rome seizes his sacramentalism and his high view of the church while burying his doctrine of grace, and modern readers psychologize his Confessions into a mere memoir of self-discovery, missing the sovereign God who is its subject.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome claims Augustine as her own and points to his sacramental and ecclesial teaching; the Reformers claimed him and pointed to his doctrine of grace. The dictionary does not pretend Augustine was a Protestant — his errors on the sacraments, the visible church, and allegory fed real later corruptions. But on the central question of how a sinner is saved, Augustine stands with Scripture against Pelagius: salvation is not of him that willeth but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16), by grace, the gift of God (Eph 2:8). Rome cannot have the doctor of grace while denying his doctrine of grace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the man, but his Confessions are often read as a mere psychological memoir, a study in the self — the first "autobiography" — with the God who is its true subject edited out. The principle to recover is that the Confessions are a prayer: a sinner confessing his sin and confessing the grace that found him. "Without me ye can do nothing" (John 15:5) is the book's heart. Augustine matters most where he points away from himself to the sovereign mercy of God.

etymology: From Roman (of the see of Rome) + catholicism (Greek katholikos, universal); the church communion under the pope of Rome.
biblical_def: Roman Catholicism is the largest body bearing the Christian name, the church communion that holds the bishop of Rome — the pope — to be the visible head of the church on earth and the successor of Peter, claiming a universal jurisdiction over all Christians. This dictionary honors what Rome has preserved: the Trinity, the deity and incarnation of Christ, the Chalcedonian faith, the Nicene Creed, the bodily resurrection, and the canon of the Old and New Testaments (though it adds the Apocrypha). These are no small things, and the dictionary will not deny that genuine Christian truth is held within the Roman communion. But Rome has also fixed, especially at the Fourth Lateran Council and the Council of Trent, doctrines the Reformation rightly called the church away from: the papal monarchy and the pope's claimed infallibility; the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice and transubstantiation; purgatory, indulgences, and the treasury of merit; the invocation of saints and the elaborate devotion to Mary, with her immaculate conception, bodily assumption, and titles as co-mediatrix; the denial of justification by faith alone; and the setting of unwritten tradition and the church's magisterium alongside Scripture as binding. This dictionary, confessing the five solas, names these as corruptions of the gospel, and holds that Trent's anathemas against justification by faith alone have never been withdrawn.
webster_summary: The church communion under the pope of Rome — preserving the Trinity, the incarnation, and the creeds, yet fixing the papal monarchy, the Mass and transubstantiation, purgatory and indulgences, Marian devotion, and the denial of justification by faith alone. The Reformation called the church away from these corruptions.
webster_full: ROMAN CATHOLICISM, noun. The church communion under the pope of Rome, claiming universal jurisdiction.
Preserves the Trinity, the deity and incarnation of Christ, and the ancient creeds.
Fixes the papal monarchy and papal infallibility; the Mass as sacrifice and transubstantiation.
Holds purgatory, indulgences, the invocation of saints, and the exalted devotion to Mary.
Denies justification by faith alone (Trent), and sets tradition alongside Scripture.

corruption_summary: Modern ecumenism urges that the Reformation dispute is over — that Rome and the heirs of the Reformers now share the gospel and differ only in emphasis; this is not true, for Rome's binding dogmas on the papacy, the Mass, merit, and justification stand unchanged, and the same gospel Paul defended is still at stake.
corruption_paragraphs: The deepest corruption of Roman Catholicism touches the gospel itself. By denying justification by faith alone and teaching a righteousness infused and increased by works and sacraments, Rome obscures the finished work of Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins for ever and sat down (Heb 10:12). By the Mass it repeats what was finished; by purgatory and indulgences it adds to what was complete; by the invocation of saints and the exalted Mary it multiplies mediators where Scripture knows but one (1 Tim 2:5); by the papacy it gives a man titles that belong to Christ alone. These are not differences of emphasis but corruptions of the faith.

This entry rebuts a named system and so uses its vocabulary plainly. The principle to recover is the five solas: Scripture alone as the binding authority, grace alone and faith alone in Christ alone for justification, to the glory of God alone. The dictionary honors the true doctrine Rome has preserved and loves the many within her communion who trust Christ, while naming her official errors for what they are. Salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, not of works (Eph 2:8) — and on that article the Reformation stands.
